purpose: Fifty Atlas-authored deep-dive and trap questions for high-yield DSA5104 concepts.

questions.commonTrap: Confusing the requested result with the execution procedure.
questions.prompt: Which statement is the best reason SQL is called declarative?
choices: The user must specify every disk read and join algorithm.
The user specifies the desired result and the DBMS chooses an execution strategy.
SQL can only be used to declare tables, never to query them.
Every SQL query is executed in exactly the same physical order.
questions.solution: SQL describes what result is required; the database system is responsible for choosing how to produce it.
questions.explanation: Declarative SQL separates logical intent from the physical execution procedure.
questions.misconception: A declarative query does not expose every implementation step to the user.
questions.visualHook: Separate the requested result from the hidden query plan.

questions.commonTrap: Treating a change to storage structures as a change to the logical schema.
questions.prompt: An administrator adds an index to student without changing table columns or application queries. Which concept does this illustrate?
choices: Logical data independence
Referential integrity
Physical data independence
View serializability
questions.solution: Adding an index changes the physical storage or access path while preserving the logical schema and applications, so it illustrates physical data independence.
questions.explanation: Physical data independence hides storage-level changes from the logical schema and user programs.
questions.misconception: Changing columns or relationships would be a logical-schema change, not merely a physical change.
questions.visualHook: Place the index below the logical schema in the abstraction stack.

questions.commonTrap: Naming the storage manager instead of the component that coordinates competing transactions.
questions.prompt: Two students try to claim the only remaining seat at the same time. Which component prevents both transactions from committing an invalid result?
choices: The file manager, because it stores the seat row
The query parser, because it checks SQL grammar
The view manager, because it hides unused columns
The concurrency-control manager within the transaction manager
questions.solution: Concurrency control coordinates interleaved transactions so that conflicting updates cannot both commit an invalid state.
questions.explanation: The transaction manager provides atomicity and coordination; concurrency control handles conflicts between concurrent transactions.
questions.misconception: Parsing a query or storing a row does not by itself serialize conflicting transactions.
questions.visualHook: Draw both registration transactions converging on one seat and mark the conflict point.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming the browser should connect directly to the database server.
questions.prompt: Why is a three-tier architecture usually preferred for a web application using a DBMS?
choices: It places presentation, application logic, and database access in separate layers.
It forces every browser to own a direct database connection.
It removes the need for authentication and authorization.
It stores all persistent data in the presentation layer.
questions.solution: Three-tier architecture separates the web presentation layer, application or business-logic layer, and database layer, which improves control and maintainability.
questions.explanation: The middle tier centralizes logic and protects the database from direct public access.
questions.misconception: Three-tier design is not a promise that the database disappears or becomes part of the browser.
questions.visualHook: Trace browser request through application server to database and back.

questions.commonTrap: Checking uniqueness but forgetting minimality.
questions.prompt: A set of attributes uniquely identifies every tuple, but one attribute can be removed and uniqueness still holds. What is the set?
choices: A candidate key but not a superkey
A superkey but not a candidate key
A foreign key only
A non-key attribute set
questions.solution: It is a superkey because it is unique, but it is not a candidate key because it is not minimal.
questions.explanation: Candidate keys are minimal superkeys.
questions.misconception: Uniqueness alone does not make a superkey minimal.
questions.visualHook: Remove one attribute from the key and retest uniqueness.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming every candidate key must be chosen as the primary key.
questions.prompt: Which statement about primary keys and candidate keys is correct?
choices: A primary key is always a proper superset of every candidate key.
A candidate key may contain duplicate tuples by definition.
A primary key is one candidate key selected to identify tuples.
A relation can have many primary keys simultaneously.
questions.solution: A relation may have several candidate keys, and one of them is selected as the primary key.
questions.explanation: Candidate keys are possible minimal identifiers; the primary key is the chosen one.
questions.misconception: Alternative candidate keys remain unique even when they are not selected as the primary key.
questions.visualHook: Show several candidate keys branching into one selected primary key.

questions.commonTrap: Checking only the child value and not the referenced parent relation.
questions.prompt: For instructor(ID, dept_name) referencing department(dept_name), which insert violates referential integrity if no such department exists?
choices: INSERT INTO department VALUES ('Physics', 500000) followed by the instructor insert
INSERT INTO instructor VALUES (102, 'Lin', NULL, 90000) when the foreign key permits NULL
An insert into an unrelated table with no foreign key
INSERT INTO instructor VALUES (101, 'Ada', 'Physics', 90000)
questions.solution: The first insert uses Physics as a non-null foreign-key value without a matching department tuple.
questions.explanation: A non-null foreign-key value must match a referenced key in the parent relation.
questions.misconception: A syntactically valid department name is not enough; the parent tuple must exist.
questions.visualHook: Draw the proposed child tuple and follow its foreign-key edge to the missing parent.

questions.commonTrap: Treating an unknown value as a valid primary-key identifier.
questions.prompt: Why can a primary-key attribute not be allowed to contain NULL?
choices: NULL does not identify a definite tuple, so uniqueness and entity identification fail.
NULL always means the value is zero.
NULL is a valid universal identifier shared by every tuple.
NULL automatically creates a foreign-key reference.
questions.solution: A primary key must identify each tuple; an unknown or nonexistent NULL value cannot provide that identity.
questions.explanation: Primary-key constraints imply both uniqueness and non-null identification.
questions.misconception: NULL is not the same as zero, an empty string, or a universal key.
questions.visualHook: Try to point two tuple rows to a concrete identity when the key cell is NULL.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming listing two relations in a product automatically matches related tuples.
questions.prompt: Which relational-algebra expression is equivalent to a theta join on predicate p?
choices: pi_p(r union s)
sigma_p(r x s)
rho_p(r - s)
r intersect s for any schemas
questions.solution: A theta join is defined as selection over the Cartesian product: sigma_p(r x s).
questions.explanation: The product creates candidate tuple pairs, and selection keeps those satisfying the join predicate.
questions.misconception: A product alone contains unrelated pairs; the predicate is the matching condition.
questions.visualHook: Show product as all pairs and selection as the filter that creates the join.

questions.commonTrap: Importing bag semantics into basic relational algebra.
questions.prompt: Under relational-algebra set semantics, what happens when projection removes attributes and makes two result tuples identical?
choices: The duplicate result tuple appears once for every source row.
The entire projection fails.
The duplicate result tuple appears only once.
The duplicate is converted to NULL.
questions.solution: Projection removes duplicate tuples under the set semantics of the relational model.
questions.explanation: SQL may preserve duplicates unless DISTINCT is requested, but classical relational algebra uses sets.
questions.misconception: SQL duplicate behavior should not be assumed for relational-algebra projection.
questions.visualHook: Collapse two projected rows with the same visible attributes into one set member.

questions.commonTrap: Checking only the number of columns and ignoring corresponding domains.
questions.prompt: Before applying relational-algebra union, what must be true?
choices: The operands have different arities so their columns can be appended.
The operands must have identical tuple counts.
One operand must always be a primary-key relation.
The operands have the same arity and compatible corresponding domains.
questions.solution: Union requires union-compatible relations: equal arity and compatible domains in corresponding positions.
questions.explanation: Union combines alternative tuples with the same tuple shape.
questions.misconception: Equal row counts are irrelevant; tuple shape and domains are the key checks.
questions.visualHook: Align the two relation headers column by column before combining rows.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming every same-named attribute is intended as a join key.
questions.prompt: Why can a natural join be dangerous in a schema that evolves over time?
choices: A newly shared attribute name can silently add an unintended join condition.
Natural join always produces a Cartesian product.
Natural join cannot combine relations with any common attribute.
Natural join always discards every unmatched tuple from both inputs.
questions.solution: Natural join joins on all same-named attributes, so a new shared name can change query semantics without changing the query text.
questions.explanation: An explicit JOIN with an ON condition makes the intended relationship visible and stable.
questions.misconception: Natural join is not simply a shorter spelling for every intended equijoin.
questions.visualHook: Add one same-named column and watch the natural-join predicate change.

questions.commonTrap: Thinking assignment changes stored database contents.
questions.prompt: What does relational-algebra assignment T <- E do?
choices: It permanently updates every stored tuple in T.
It names the result of expression E as an intermediate relation T.
It creates a foreign-key constraint from E to T.
It deletes all tuples that are not produced by E.
questions.solution: Assignment binds the relation-valued result of E to a name T for use in later expressions; it is not a database mutation.
questions.explanation: Assignment improves readability and supports multi-step relational-algebra expressions.
questions.misconception: A named intermediate result is different from an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.
questions.visualHook: Draw E flowing into a temporary named box T, not into persistent storage.

questions.commonTrap: Calling any split that removes columns a correct decomposition.
questions.prompt: Which pair of goals best describes a good decomposition of a redundant relation?
choices: Create more duplicate facts and prevent the original information from being reconstructed.
Replace all keys with NULL and avoid every join.
Reduce repeated facts while preserving the information recoverable by the intended join.
Store every attribute in every new relation to guarantee repetition.
questions.solution: A useful decomposition reduces redundancy and remains lossless with respect to the information represented by the original relation.
questions.explanation: Good design balances anomaly reduction with information preservation.
questions.misconception: Fewer columns alone do not prove that a decomposition is lossless.
questions.visualHook: Compare the repeated department facts before the split and the join reconstruction after it.

questions.commonTrap: Treating a schema change as a row-level mutation.
questions.prompt: Which statement changes the relation schema rather than only the current relation instance?
choices: INSERT INTO student (ID, name) VALUES (1, 'Lin')
`DELETE FROM student WHERE ID = 1`
`UPDATE student SET name = 'Lin' WHERE ID = 1`
ALTER TABLE student ADD email VARCHAR(100)
questions.solution: ALTER TABLE changes the table definition; INSERT, DELETE, and UPDATE change stored rows.
questions.explanation: DDL defines or changes database objects, while DML manipulates the current instance.
questions.misconception: Both DDL and DML are SQL, but they act at different levels.
questions.visualHook: Put ALTER TABLE on the schema side and the other statements on the data side.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming foreign-key validation is only a type check.
questions.prompt: A table takes(ID, course_id) references student(ID). Which insert is valid only if student 99999 already exists?
choices: INSERT INTO takes VALUES (99999, 'CS-101')
INSERT INTO student VALUES (99999, 'Kai', 'Comp. Sci.', 0)
INSERT INTO takes VALUES (NULL, 'CS-101') when ID is nullable
INSERT INTO course VALUES ('CS-101', 'Intro', 'Comp. Sci.', 3)
questions.solution: The takes insert requires a matching student row for ID 99999 unless the foreign-key value is NULL and NULL is permitted.
questions.explanation: Referential integrity checks the existence of the referenced parent key.
questions.misconception: A value having the right data type does not make it a valid foreign-key reference.
questions.visualHook: Follow takes.ID to the parent student.ID row.

questions.commonTrap: Confusing cascading child deletion with cascading parent deletion.
questions.prompt: If `takes.student_id` references `student.id` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, what happens when a referenced student is deleted?
choices: The student deletion is always rejected, regardless of child rows.
Matching takes rows are deleted automatically.
Every student row is deleted.
The student ID is replaced with a random value in takes.
questions.solution: The cascade action removes child rows in takes whose foreign key points to the deleted student.
questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE propagates a parent deletion to matching referencing rows.
questions.misconception: Cascade is a defined referential action, not a command to delete unrelated rows.
questions.visualHook: Animate one parent row deletion along its reference edges to child rows.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming a CHECK constraint automatically makes every column non-null.
questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a CHECK (credits BETWEEN 0 AND 6) constraint?
choices: Create a foreign key to the course table.
Guarantee that every course title is unique.
Restrict non-NULL credits values to the declared range.
Delete rows whose credits are outside the range.
questions.solution: A CHECK predicate constrains values that are evaluated for the row; a separate NOT NULL constraint is needed when NULL must be forbidden.
questions.explanation: CHECK expresses a row-level condition and does not replace every other integrity constraint.
questions.misconception: Range validity, nullability, and uniqueness are different constraints.
questions.visualHook: Separate the value-range gate from the NOT NULL and UNIQUE gates.

questions.commonTrap: Using UPDATE when the requested change is to the table definition.
questions.prompt: The request is to add a phone column to every future and existing student row. Which operation changes the schema?
choices: `UPDATE student SET phone = NULL`
INSERT INTO student (ID, name) VALUES (1, 'Lin')
SELECT phone FROM student
ALTER TABLE student ADD phone VARCHAR(30)
questions.solution: Adding a column is a schema operation, so ALTER TABLE is the appropriate statement.
questions.explanation: UPDATE can populate an existing column but cannot introduce a column into the table definition.
questions.misconception: Changing values in rows is not the same as changing the set of attributes.
questions.visualHook: Show the column appearing in the schema before any row values are populated.

questions.commonTrap: Putting an aggregate condition in WHERE.
questions.prompt: You need departments whose average instructor salary exceeds 90000. Where should that aggregate condition normally go?
choices: In HAVING, after grouping by department.
In WHERE, before rows are grouped.
In ORDER BY, because averages are sorted.
In FROM, because aggregates define tables.
questions.solution: Use GROUP BY dept_name HAVING AVG(salary) > 90000; WHERE filters individual input rows before grouping.
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after aggregate values have been computed.
questions.misconception: WHERE and HAVING are not interchangeable when the predicate depends on an aggregate.
questions.visualHook: Place WHERE before the grouping box and HAVING after it.

questions.commonTrap: Using DISTINCT without understanding the multiplicity created by a join.
questions.prompt: A student takes five sections, and a query joins student to takes. Why can the student name appear five times?
choices: SQL always duplicates every selected column five times.
The join produces one result row per matching student-takes pair.
The primary key of student is ignored by every query.
GROUP BY automatically expands one student into five rows.
questions.solution: A one-to-many join returns a row for each matching takes tuple, so the student is repeated once per section.
questions.explanation: Duplicate output reflects join cardinality; DISTINCT may collapse names but can also hide useful multiplicity.
questions.misconception: A primary key identifies the student row but does not prevent multiple joined result rows.
questions.visualHook: Connect one student node to five takes nodes and count the result pairs.

questions.commonTrap: Swapping the duplicate behavior of UNION and UNION ALL.
questions.prompt: Which operator removes duplicate rows between two union-compatible query results?
choices: UNION ALL
INTERSECT ALL
UNION
CROSS JOIN
questions.solution: UNION combines compatible results with duplicate elimination; UNION ALL preserves duplicates.
questions.explanation: Choose UNION ALL when multiplicity matters and UNION when set-style duplicate removal is intended.
questions.misconception: The word ALL is the signal that duplicates are retained.
questions.visualHook: Merge two result streams and mark whether repeated tuples survive.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming LIKE is case-insensitive in every SQL system.
questions.prompt: Which predicate is the safest course-style way to find department names containing sci regardless of case?
choices: dept_name = 'sci'
dept_name LIKE 'sci'
UPPER(dept_name) = '%sci%'
LOWER(dept_name) LIKE '%sci%'
questions.solution: Applying LOWER to the column and comparing with a lowercase wildcard pattern makes the intended case-insensitive match explicit.
questions.explanation: The wildcard pattern needs % for arbitrary characters; LOWER normalizes the comparison side.
questions.misconception: Equality and LIKE have different wildcard semantics, and case behavior can be dialect-dependent.
questions.visualHook: Normalize both the stored value and the search pattern before matching.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming COUNT(column) counts NULL values.
questions.prompt: For a group with five rows, two of which have grade IS NULL, which statement is correct?
choices: COUNT(*) returns 5, while COUNT(grade) returns 3.
COUNT(*) and COUNT(grade) both return 3.
COUNT(*) returns 3, while COUNT(grade) returns 5.
Both counts return NULL.
questions.solution: COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(grade) counts only non-NULL grade values.
questions.explanation: The distinction is essential when measuring enrollment or completion with nullable attributes.
questions.misconception: COUNT(column) does not count the row merely because the row exists.
questions.visualHook: Count row boxes for COUNT(*) and non-empty grade cells for COUNT(grade).

questions.commonTrap: Replacing a LEFT JOIN with an INNER JOIN and losing entities with no match.
questions.prompt: You must list every instructor, including instructors who teach no section. Which join starts with the correct preservation behavior?
choices: `instructor INNER JOIN teaches ON instructor.ID = teaches.ID`
`instructor LEFT OUTER JOIN teaches ON instructor.ID = teaches.ID`
instructor CROSS JOIN teaches
instructor UNION teaches
questions.solution: A left outer join preserves every row from instructor and supplies NULLs for missing teaches matches.
questions.explanation: The preserved side of the outer join is the side whose unmatched rows must remain.
questions.misconception: An inner join removes instructors without a matching teaches row.
questions.visualHook: Keep every instructor card visible and attach a NULL teaches side when unmatched.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming all columns with the same name carry the same relationship meaning.
questions.prompt: What is the best repair when a natural join is sensitive to an accidental same-named column?
choices: Add more same-named columns so the join becomes more specific.
Use SELECT * and trust the DBMS to infer business meaning.
Replace it with an explicit JOIN with an ON condition naming the intended keys.
Convert the join to UNION ALL.
questions.solution: An explicit ON predicate states exactly which attributes define the relationship and prevents accidental same-name predicates.
questions.explanation: Explicit join conditions make query semantics robust to unrelated schema additions.
questions.misconception: Natural join derives intent from names, not from the business relationship.
questions.visualHook: Circle the intended key pair in an explicit ON clause.

sourceRefs.role: deep-dive trap derived from teacher homework

questions.commonTrap: Listing tables in FROM without connecting their related keys.
questions.prompt: A query uses FROM student, takes but has no condition connecting the two tables. What is the likely problem?
choices: It automatically performs a correct primary-key join.
It returns only students with no takes rows.
It is equivalent to a LEFT OUTER JOIN.
It forms a Cartesian product and pairs unrelated rows.
questions.solution: Without a join predicate, every student is paired with every takes row, producing a Cartesian product.
questions.explanation: The query needs a condition such as `student.ID = takes.ID` to express the relationship.
questions.misconception: Comma-separated tables do not infer every intended foreign-key relationship.
questions.visualHook: Compare all student-times-takes pairings with only matching ID pairs.

questions.commonTrap: Putting a right-side condition in WHERE and removing NULL-extended rows.
questions.prompt: Why can a LEFT JOIN followed by WHERE right.value = 'x' behave like an inner join?
choices: The WHERE predicate rejects the NULL-extended rows created for unmatched right tuples.
LEFT JOIN always ignores its left input.
WHERE runs before the join and changes the join type directly.
The right table is duplicated before filtering.
questions.solution: Unmatched left rows receive NULL on the right, and right.value = 'x' is not TRUE for those rows, so WHERE removes them.
questions.explanation: To preserve unmatched rows while filtering matches, move the right-side condition into the ON clause when appropriate.
questions.misconception: Outer-join preservation can be undone by a later null-rejecting predicate.
questions.visualHook: Mark the NULL right-side row and watch it fail the WHERE predicate.

sourceRefs.role: deep-dive trap derived from teacher homework

questions.commonTrap: Assuming MySQL supports FULL OUTER JOIN exactly like some other systems.
questions.prompt: What is a common MySQL-compatible pattern for simulating a FULL OUTER JOIN between a and b?
choices: Replace both tables with CROSS JOIN.
Combine a LEFT JOIN and a reversed LEFT JOIN with UNION.
Use UNION ALL without any join predicates.
Use only NATURAL JOIN and rely on NULL padding.
questions.solution: A common workaround is the union of a LEFT JOIN b and b LEFT JOIN a, with duplicate handling chosen deliberately.
questions.explanation: MySQL does not provide a direct FULL OUTER JOIN keyword, so the two preserved sides must be combined.
questions.misconception: A Cartesian product is not an outer join, and UNION alone does not create matching logic.
questions.visualHook: Preserve unmatched rows from A in one half and unmatched rows from B in the reversed half.

sourceRefs.role: deep-dive trap derived from teacher homework

questions.commonTrap: Assuming joining on a key always produces one output row.
questions.prompt: If one instructor teaches three sections and the query joins instructor to teaches on instructor ID, how many matching joined rows represent that instructor?
choices: One, because instructor ID is a primary key
Zero, because teaches has a composite key
Three, one for each matching teaches row
One for every instructor in the database
questions.solution: The primary key identifies one instructor input row, but the one-to-many relationship creates one output row per matching teaches row.
questions.explanation: Key uniqueness on one side does not prevent multiplicity from the other side.
questions.misconception: A key controls identification, not the number of related tuples in a join.
questions.visualHook: Connect one instructor node to three section nodes and count edges.

sourceRefs.role: deep-dive trap derived from teacher homework

questions.commonTrap: Expecting both copies of the USING column in the result.
questions.prompt: What is a key output difference between JOIN USING (ID) and an unconstrained Cartesian product?
choices: USING discards every non-ID column.
USING creates every possible row pair before filtering.
USING is only valid for tables with no common column.
USING joins equal ID values and presents the common ID as one merged column.
questions.solution: USING names the common join column, matches equal values, and avoids two separate copies of that common column in the output.
questions.explanation: USING is a concise form for an equality join on named common attributes.
questions.misconception: USING is not a synonym for CROSS JOIN and does not erase unrelated attributes.
questions.visualHook: Merge the two ID header cells after matching equal values.

sourceRefs.role: deep-dive trap derived from teacher homework

questions.commonTrap: Treating `NULL = NULL` as TRUE.
questions.prompt: What is the truth value of `NULL = NULL` in SQL's three-valued logic?
choices: UNKNOWN
TRUE
FALSE
It depends on whether NULL is numeric
questions.solution: Comparisons involving NULL produce UNKNOWN because NULL represents an unknown or inapplicable value, not an ordinary comparable value.
questions.explanation: Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test nullness explicitly.
questions.misconception: NULL is not an ordinary value that can equal another NULL.
questions.visualHook: Route a NULL comparison to the UNKNOWN branch, not TRUE or FALSE.

questions.commonTrap: Ignoring NULL in the subquery result.
questions.prompt: Why can x NOT IN (subquery) unexpectedly return no rows when the subquery contains NULL?
choices: NOT IN always means equality with NULL.
The comparison can become UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE.
The subquery is executed after the outer query is deleted.
NULL is treated as a wildcard matching every x.
questions.solution: A NULL in the list makes a non-matching comparison UNKNOWN under three-valued logic, so the NOT IN predicate may fail to be TRUE.
questions.explanation: When NULL is possible, a carefully correlated NOT EXISTS formulation is often safer.
questions.misconception: NOT IN is not simply a mechanical negation of IN when NULL participates.
questions.visualHook: Show one NULL candidate contaminating the final conjunction with UNKNOWN.

questions.commonTrap: Writing equality against NULL instead of using IS NULL.
questions.prompt: Which predicate correctly selects rows whose advisor ID is missing?
choices: advisor_id = NULL
advisor_id == NULL
advisor_id IS NULL
advisor_id IN (NULL)
questions.solution: Use IS NULL to test whether an attribute contains NULL.
questions.explanation: Equality comparisons with NULL produce UNKNOWN instead of performing a nullness test.
questions.misconception: SQL uses IS NULL and IS NOT NULL for nullness checks.
questions.visualHook: Use a dedicated NULL test gate rather than an equality comparator.

questions.commonTrap: Assuming AVG includes NULL as a zero.
questions.prompt: For values 10, 20, and NULL, what does SQL conceptually use for AVG(value)?
choices: The average of 10, 20, and zero, namely 10.
NULL because any NULL poisons every aggregate.
The value 30 because AVG is an alias for SUM.
The average of non-NULL values, namely 15.
questions.solution: Most SQL aggregates such as AVG ignore NULL inputs, so the average is computed from 10 and 20.
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) differs from COUNT(column), and aggregate NULL behavior must be checked when interpreting results.
questions.misconception: Ignoring NULL is different from treating NULL as numeric zero.
questions.visualHook: Remove the NULL cell from the aggregate input set before computing the mean.

questions.commonTrap: Selecting a non-aggregated column that is not grouped.
questions.prompt: Why is `SELECT dept_name, name, AVG(salary) FROM instructor GROUP BY dept_name` problematic in standard SQL?
choices: name is neither aggregated nor included in GROUP BY.
AVG cannot be used with GROUP BY.
dept_name must be removed from SELECT.
GROUP BY can only group numeric columns.
questions.solution: Each selected non-aggregated column must be grouped or otherwise determined by the group; name is not specified at the department-group level.
questions.explanation: A department group can contain many instructor names, so one name is not determined by the group.
questions.misconception: GROUP BY does not choose an arbitrary representative for every ungrouped selected column.
questions.visualHook: Put all instructors in one department bucket and ask which single name should be returned.

questions.commonTrap: Filtering rows after grouping when the condition should reduce input rows first.
questions.prompt: You want the average salary of instructors with salary above 70000, grouped by department. Which shape is correct?
choices: `HAVING salary > 70000 with no grouping condition.`
`WHERE salary > 70000 before GROUP BY, then AVG(salary).`
`ORDER BY salary > 70000 before computing AVG.`
`DISTINCT salary > 70000 in the SELECT list.`
questions.solution: Use WHERE to discard low-salary input rows before grouping, then compute AVG for each remaining department group.
questions.explanation: HAVING is for conditions on groups or aggregate results; WHERE is for row-level input filters.
questions.misconception: A row predicate and a group predicate can produce different averages even when they use similar words.
questions.visualHook: Filter individual rows first, then place the survivors into department groups.

questions.commonTrap: Counting enrollment rows instead of unique students.
questions.prompt: A student can retake a course. Which expression counts unique students who appear in takes?
choices: COUNT(*)
COUNT(course_id)
COUNT(DISTINCT ID)
SUM(ID)
questions.solution: COUNT(DISTINCT ID) counts each student ID once even when the student has multiple takes rows.
questions.explanation: The DISTINCT applies before counting, which removes repeated IDs from the aggregate input.
questions.misconception: COUNT(*) measures rows, not necessarily entities.
questions.visualHook: Deduplicate repeated student IDs before applying COUNT.

questions.commonTrap: Reading SELECT as if it is evaluated first.
questions.prompt: Which sequence best matches the logical order for a grouped SELECT query?
choices: SELECT, FROM/JOIN, ORDER BY, WHERE, HAVING, GROUP BY
WHERE, SELECT, FROM/JOIN, HAVING, GROUP BY, ORDER BY
ORDER BY, SELECT, GROUP BY, FROM/JOIN, WHERE, HAVING
FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY
questions.solution: The logical pipeline forms rows, filters rows, groups them, filters groups, projects the select list, and finally orders the result.
questions.explanation: This order explains why WHERE cannot normally reference an aggregate that exists only after grouping.
questions.misconception: The textual position of SELECT does not mean SELECT is logically evaluated first.
questions.visualHook: Build the query as a six-stage pipeline from rows to ordered output.

questions.commonTrap: Expecting one global aggregate when GROUP BY creates one aggregate per group.
questions.prompt: What does `SELECT dept_name, COUNT(*) FROM instructor GROUP BY dept_name` return?
choices: One row per department with that department's instructor count.
One row for every instructor and the global instructor count.
One row containing only the largest department.
A single row with no department name.
questions.solution: GROUP BY partitions instructors by department, and COUNT is computed separately within each department.
questions.explanation: The grouped column identifies the result groups; the aggregate summarizes each group.
questions.misconception: Adding a grouping column changes the scope of the aggregate from global to per-group.
questions.visualHook: Sort instructors into department buckets and count each bucket separately.

questions.commonTrap: Checking whether at least one related row satisfies a condition instead of all required rows.
questions.prompt: Which query shape best expresses find instructors who teach every course offered by their department?
choices: Use EXISTS to find one course the instructor teaches.
Use NOT EXISTS to find a department course that the instructor does not teach.
Use COUNT(*) without comparing it to the department's course count.
Use ORDER BY course_id and take the first row.
questions.solution: The standard every-pattern is to reject an instructor when there exists a required course for which no matching teaching row exists.
questions.explanation: Every can be expressed as NOT EXISTS of a counterexample.
questions.misconception: EXISTS proves at least one match, not that all required matches are present.
questions.visualHook: Search for a single missing required course; one counterexample eliminates the instructor.

questions.commonTrap: Ignoring correlation when replacing EXISTS with IN.
questions.prompt: What is the key semantic difference between an uncorrelated IN subquery and a correlated EXISTS subquery?
choices: IN always updates the inner table, while EXISTS only reads it.
EXISTS cannot contain a WHERE clause.
EXISTS can refer to the current outer row through a correlation predicate; IN compares with a produced set.
IN and EXISTS always produce identical NULL behavior.
questions.solution: A correlated EXISTS evaluates whether a matching inner row exists for the current outer row; IN usually tests membership in a subquery result.
questions.explanation: The correlation predicate is what ties the nested query to each outer tuple.
questions.misconception: IN and EXISTS can be equivalent in some cases, but their semantics and NULL behavior must not be assumed identical.
questions.visualHook: Draw an outer row pointer entering the inner query for correlated EXISTS.

questions.commonTrap: Swapping SOME and ALL comparison meaning.
questions.prompt: For a non-empty subquery result, what does `x > ALL (subquery)` require?
choices: x is greater than at least one value returned by the subquery.
x equals one of the values returned by the subquery.
The subquery must return exactly one row.
x is greater than every value returned by the subquery.
questions.solution: ALL requires the comparison to hold for every value in the subquery result; SOME or ANY requires at least one.
questions.explanation: Quantifier words change the number of inner values that must satisfy the comparison.
questions.misconception: ALL is stronger than SOME/ANY and is not a synonym for a scalar subquery.
questions.visualHook: Test x against each inner value and require every comparison to pass.

questions.commonTrap: Forgetting the NULL caveat when applying an algebraic equivalence.
questions.prompt: Ignoring NULL complications, which quantified comparison is equivalent to x NOT IN (subquery)?
choices: x <> ALL (subquery)
`x = ALL (subquery)`
x <> SOME (subquery)
`x = ANY (subquery)`
questions.solution: NOT IN means x differs from every returned value, which is expressed as x <> ALL(subquery) when NULL behavior is excluded.
questions.explanation: With NULL values, three-valued logic can make the practical behavior surprising; the equivalence must be used carefully.
questions.misconception: x <> SOME only requires one different value and is therefore much weaker.
questions.visualHook: Compare x against every member of the subquery result, not just one member.

questions.commonTrap: Using a multi-row subquery where a single value is required.
questions.prompt: What must be true when a subquery is used as a scalar value in an expression such as `salary > (subquery)`?
choices: The subquery must return one row for every outer row.
The subquery must return at most one value.
The subquery must return a table with at least two columns.
The subquery must contain GROUP BY.
questions.solution: A scalar subquery is expected to produce one value; multiple rows generally cause an error unless the query is rewritten with a quantified operator or aggregate.
questions.explanation: Use IN, SOME, ALL, EXISTS, or an aggregate when the inner query is intentionally multi-row.
questions.misconception: Parentheses around a subquery do not automatically reduce many rows to one value.
questions.visualHook: Check the cardinality of the inner result before plugging it into a single comparison slot.

questions.commonTrap: Writing EXISTS when the question requires absence of a counterexample.
questions.prompt: The statement student has taken every required course is most safely implemented as what logical pattern?
choices: There exists at least one required course the student has taken.
The student has taken a course with the maximum course ID.
There does not exist a required course that the student has not taken.
The student appears in the takes table at least once.
questions.solution: Every can be rewritten as NOT EXISTS a required item for which the student's matching row is absent.
questions.explanation: Searching for a counterexample is the standard SQL translation of a universal condition.
questions.misconception: At least one match is an existential condition and is insufficient for every.
questions.visualHook: Keep a student only when the search for a missing required course returns empty.

questions.commonTrap: Treating a CTE as a permanent table.
questions.prompt: What is the usual scope of a non-recursive CTE introduced with WITH?
choices: It permanently creates a table in the database catalog.
It changes the schema of every referenced relation.
It is available to every future database session.
It names a query result for the single statement that follows.
questions.solution: A CTE is a named query expression scoped to the statement that follows the WITH clause.
questions.explanation: Use CREATE VIEW or CREATE TABLE when a reusable persistent database object is intended.
questions.misconception: A readable named subquery is not automatically a materialized or permanent relation.
questions.visualHook: Draw the CTE name inside one statement boundary and stop its lifetime at the semicolon.

questions.commonTrap: Omitting the anchor member or writing a recursive member that cannot make progress.
questions.prompt: Which pair is required for a recursive CTE that walks prerequisite edges?
choices: An anchor query for starting courses and a recursive query that expands to more prerequisites.
Two unrelated INSERT statements.
Only an ORDER BY clause and a final SELECT.
A permanent table and a foreign-key cascade.
questions.solution: The anchor member seeds the result, and the recursive member joins the current frontier to discover additional prerequisite rows.
questions.explanation: A recursive CTE needs a base case and an expansion step; the data or predicate must eventually stop producing new rows.
questions.misconception: RECURSIVE does not mean the DBMS guesses a starting row or termination rule.
questions.visualHook: Show the anchor as level zero and each recursive expansion as the next graph frontier.

questions.commonTrap: Computing an average over raw instructors instead of over department totals.
questions.prompt: Why use a CTE for departments whose total salary exceeds the average department total?
choices: The CTE forces every department to have the same salary.
The CTE first creates one total per department, which the outer query can average.
The CTE converts all rows into a permanent index.
The CTE removes the need for GROUP BY in every query.
questions.solution: The inner grouped result produces department totals; the outer query can then compute the average of those totals and compare each department with it.
questions.explanation: The intermediate relation makes the two aggregation levels explicit.
questions.misconception: Average of department totals is not necessarily the same as average of all instructor salaries.
questions.visualHook: Build department-total rows first, then compute a second-level average over those rows.

questions.commonTrap: Using CTE as a claim that the result is automatically faster or persistent.
questions.prompt: What is the most defensible reason to introduce a CTE in a complex query?
choices: To guarantee that the DBMS materializes the result on disk.
To guarantee that the query uses an index.
To give a meaningful name to an intermediate relation-valued expression.
To turn a SELECT into an atomic transaction.
questions.solution: A CTE improves structure and readability by naming an intermediate query result; performance and materialization depend on the DBMS and query.
questions.explanation: CTEs clarify multi-stage logic without promising a particular physical plan.
questions.misconception: Syntax that improves readability is not automatically a performance hint or transaction boundary.
questions.visualHook: Replace a long nested expression with a named intermediate box and keep the same data flow.
